clinicalPearls: Presents as tender, erythematous, non-ulcerating nodules typically over the bilateral pretibial surfaces, sometimes extending to knees, ankles, or extensor forearms
Lesions evolve in color like a bruise (bright red to violaceous to yellow-green) over 1-2 weeks without ulcerating or scarring
Often accompanied by fever, malaise, arthralgia, and sometimes frank arthritis of ankles/knees
Far more common in women, with peak incidence in the second to fourth decades of life
Most cases are idiopathic or post-streptococcal, but a broad secondary workup is warranted, especially with atypical features
Lesions are typically bilateral and symmetric; unilateral or ulcerating nodules should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Represents a hypersensitivity reaction pattern rather than a single disease, so the search for an underlying trigger is central to management
Usually self-limited, resolving over 3-6 weeks even without treatment of an identifiable cause
harrison.pathophysiology: Erythema nodosum is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction resulting in inflammation centered on the subcutaneous fat septae (septal panniculitis), triggered by circulating immune complexes or antigen-driven T-cell responses to a variety of infectious, inflammatory, or drug antigens. The septal inflammatory infiltrate initially contains neutrophils and later becomes predominantly lymphohistiocytic with multinucleated giant cells, without primary vasculitis. The overlying epidermis and dermis are typically spared, which explains the absence of ulceration or scarring despite the deep tenderness.
additionalDifferentials: Nodular vasculitis / erythema induratum (lobular panniculitis, often with ulceration, seen more on posterior calves)
Insect bite reaction or panniculitis from trauma
infectionMimics: Tuberculosis-related erythema nodosum (erythema induratum can mimic classic EN)
Deep fungal infection (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis) presenting with tender nodules
Cat-scratch disease with nodular skin lesions
nonInfectiousMimics: Sarcoidosis (with or without Löfgren syndrome triad of EN, hilar adenopathy, and arthritis)
Drug hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., to sulfonamides, oral contraceptives)
additionalInvestigations: Throat culture and antistreptolysin O titer — screen for antecedent streptococcal infection, the most common identifiable trigger
Chest radiograph — evaluate for hilar lymphadenopathy suggesting sarcoidosis or for findings of tuberculosis
Complete blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) — assess systemic inflammatory activity, often markedly elevated
Stool studies or IBD-directed workup if gastrointestinal symptoms present — assess for inflammatory bowel disease
Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay — evaluate for underlying tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions
Medication history review — identify possible drug-induced etiology
Skin biopsy (deep incisional, including subcutaneous fat) — confirms septal panniculitis when diagnosis is uncertain or lesions are atypical
Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age — pregnancy is a recognized trigger
redFlags: Ulcerating, unilateral, or persistent nodules beyond 6-8 weeks, suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as nodular vasculitis or vasculitic panniculitis
Significant weight loss, chronic cough, or night sweats raising concern for tuberculosis or malignancy
Bloody diarrhea or chronic abdominal symptoms suggesting undiagnosed inflammatory bowel disease
Marked hilar adenopathy on imaging warranting evaluation for sarcoidosis or lymphoma
Recurrent or refractory episodes despite removal of an identified trigger, warranting rheumatologic referral
pitfalls: Assuming erythema nodosum is always idiopathic without pursuing a directed search for streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, tuberculosis, or drug causes
Confusing erythema nodosum with nodular vasculitis/erythema induratum, which favors the posterior calf and can ulcerate, changing management implications
Overlooking Löfgren syndrome (EN plus bilateral hilar adenopathy and arthritis) as a distinct, generally self-limited sarcoid presentation with a favorable prognosis
Performing a superficial punch biopsy instead of a deep incisional biopsy, which may miss the septal panniculitis needed for histologic confirmation
harrison.prognosis: Erythema nodosum is typically self-limited, with lesions resolving spontaneously over 3-6 weeks without scarring, though it may recur if the underlying trigger persists or recurs. Prognosis is generally excellent and closely tied to management of any identified underlying condition.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Skin Manifestations of Internal Disease (Panniculitis/Erythema Nodosum)
management: Identify and treat the underlying trigger — antecedent streptococcal infection, a culprit drug, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or inflammatory bowel disease
Relieve symptoms with rest, leg elevation, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and inflammation
Use compression stockings to reduce lower-limb discomfort and swelling
For persistent or refractory lesions, consider potassium iodide or colchicine once infection has been excluded
Reserve systemic corticosteroids for severe refractory cases after excluding underlying infection and malignancy
Reassure that lesions are self-limiting and resolve without scarring, while investigating recurrence for a persistent underlying cause
